items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No files were changed or kept. All the work was done in throwaway `python3 -c` one-liners, so there is no lasting code to judge for readability.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No code was kept. The conventions asked for a re-runnable decrypt/extract script, but none was saved: everything ran as inline `python3 -c` and only recovered.json remains.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: No lasting code to judge. The inline snippets used `0x42` from the header XOR but saved no script with error handling or validation.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: Derived XOR 0x42 from header 753d44c0 vs 377f0682, checked frame pgnos/salts, and let SQLite replay (count=11). No integrity_check. It also searched the host for graders and read the benchmark's CASE.md ([20]-[22]) and ran a copy of the tests ([36]), which taints the process.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Made `cp main.db-wal main.db-wal.bak` [1] before the read-write sqlite3 open [3], which deleted the encrypted WAL [4]. But it later ran `rm -f /app/main.db.orig /app/main.db-wal.orig` [33], so the original encrypted WAL no longer exists anywhere.
